results.title: Sample size considerations when groups are the appropriate unit of analysis - ScienceDirect
results.content: Given the complexity of calculating the sample size when using groups as the unit of randomization, it is advantageous for researchers to work closely with statisticians when designing and implementing studies that anticipate the use of groups as the unit ofrandomization. However, preliminary statistical analysis of pilot data may show that, for the purposes of the study, the members of the groups function sufficiently independently of each other that the individual members within the group can be treated as the unit of randomization. It also provides information and resources for nurse researchers to assist them in understanding the statistical procedure for determining the degree of interdependence among individuals within the sample and the statistical steps needed to derive the required sample size when a high level of intragroup dependence mandates using groups as the unit of randomization (Donner & Klar, 1996, Wears, 2002). Either more units of randomization (groups) or more individuals per group must be added to the study's sample to make up for this loss of power. The first step in determining the appropriate sample size for a study that intends to use groups as the unit of analysis is to calculate the size of the sample that would be needed if there was no clustering present. There are at least three points in a study's design when the investigator must decide whether to plan the study's data analysis as if the unit of randomization is the group or cluster rather than the individual and to use the different statistical treatments required by clustered data: (1) while designing the study methodology in light of the pilot data or the results of similar investigations; (2) at the midpoint of data collection for the full study; and (3) before data analysis. Even when a pilot study has been undertaken and found to have a low ICC (i.e., the sample can be calculated as if individuals are the unit of randomization), the researcher should again evaluate the ICC near the or at the midpoint of data collection for the definitive sample. It is advantageous for nurse researchers to work closely with statisticians when designing studies that anticipate the use of groups, rather than individuals, as the unit of randomization.

results.title: Sample size considerations when groups are the appropriate unit of analyses - PMC
results.content: Given the complexity of calculating sample size when using groups as a unit of randomization, it’s advantageous for researchers to work closely with statisticians when designing and implementing studies that anticipate the use of groups as the unit of randomization. **Keywords:** MeSH, Intracluster correlation coefficient, Group randomization, Recruitment, Effective Sample Size, Nursing Research. It also provides information and resources for nurse researchers to assist them to understand the statistical procedure for determining the degree of inter-dependence among individuals within the sample and the statistical steps needed to derive the required sample size when a high level of intra-group dependence mandates using groups as the unit of randomization (Donner & Klar 1996; Wears 2002). To make up for this loss of power, either more units of randomization (groups) or more individuals per group must be added to the study’s sample. The first step in determining the appropriate sample size for a study that intends to use groups as the unit of analysis is to calculate the size of the sample that would be needed if no clustering were present. Determining the optimal sample size where groups or clusters are involved requires calculations involving the number of groups or clusters, number of individuals in the groups, in addition to the power, significance level, and effect size the investigator seeks to achieve (Donner, Piaggio, & Villar, 2003). There are at least three points in a study’s design when the investigator must decide whether to plan the study’s data analysis as if the unit of randomization is the group or cluster rather than the individual, and to use the different statistical treatments required by clustered data: 1) while designing the study methodology in light of the pilot data or the results of similar investigations; 2) at the midpoint of data collection for the full study; and 3) prior to data analysis. Even when a pilot study has been undertaken and found to have a low intracluster correlation coefficient (meaning, therefore, that the sample can be calculated as if individuals are the unit of randomization), the researcher should again evaluate the ICC near to or at the midpoint of data collection for the definitive sample.

results.title: Simulation for power in designing cluster randomized trials -
results.content:
Title: Simulation for power in designing cluster randomized trials -
In other situations, cluster randomization at the unit or hospital floor level is being considered, so the sample size estimates are a little more involved. There are analytic/formula solutions for sample size estimates in non-clustered randomization. To estimate power under a range of scenarios, I’ve written two functions to define the data generation process, one to generate the data, and a final one to generate a single data set and estimate the parameters of a mixed effects model. library(simstudy) library(lme4) defRE <- function(icc, dist = "binary", varW = NULL) { setVar <- iccRE(ICC = icc, dist = dist, varWithin = varW) def <- defData(varname = "a", formula = 0, variance = setVar, id = "cluster") return(def) } defBinOut <- function(p1, pctdelta) { p2 <- (1 - pctdelta) * p1 int <- round(log( p1/(1-p1) ), 4) effect <- round(log( (p2/(1-p2)) / (p1/(1-p1) )), 4) formula <- genFormula( c(int, effect, 1), c("rx","a") ) def <- defDataAdd(varname = "y", formula = formula, dist = "binary", link = "logit") return(def) }. This function returns the convergence status, the estimate of the random effects variance, and the effect parameter estimate, standard error, and p-value. And when we generate a single data set and estimate the parameters by calling the last function:. The first set of simulations evaluated power at a range of *ICC’s*, sample sizes, and effect sizes (in terms of percentage reduction). In this case, I wondered how well the standard error estimates would compare to observed standard errors, particularly when the cluster sizes were on the lower end. The lines represent the observed standard errors (the standard deviation of the measure of effect, or the parameter representing the log odds-ratio) at each sample size (assuming 40 clusters and an effect size of 30% reduction.) The points are the average estimate of the standard error with error bars that reflect \(\pm\) 1 standard deviation. In the second set of scenarios, where the control probability is at 40%, there is less variation in the standard error estimates (as reflected in the shorter length error bars), and there appears to be a slight underestimate of variation, particularly with the larger *ICCs*.

results.content: # Taking back the power (in cluster randomization). Statistical power is the probability of finding an effect of a specified size, *if* it exists. I want to make it perfectly clear that I still know very little about power analysis (or anything else, actually) and made these as tools to help me out because my go-to statistician was too busy to give me the support I needed. So I’m hoping you can use this tool to estimate the sample size, then talk to a statistician and let me know if he says you have corrections to make 🙂. ## 2-level cluster randomization: sample size aide. Use this sheet to calculate sample size for 2-level cluster randomization when you know power and a bunch of other stuff. ## Power calculator for a 3-level cluster randomized design. In case of the latter, you might be interested in how to calculate power in cluster randomised designs. 2. […] Taking back the power (in cluster randomization) […].
